name: Telefol
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 7.3 STRESS. The author has not been able to detect any consistent and marked differences in loudness between the syllables of a word. On various occasions "stress" has been noted, but later checking has shown that such observations were in fact falling pitches, high pitches, or phonetically long vowels, all of which are features associated with Australian English "stressed" syllables. [p. 26, section 7:] The analysis adopted in this paper involves two tonemes, an UP toneme marked with an acute accent, and a DOWN toneme marked with a grave accent. [7.1:] Each short syllable-nucleus carries or contains one toneme, except for a few contracted syllables which carry two tonemes.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Telefol is a tone language (two tonemes, UP and DOWN, one per short syllable nucleus, freely combining within the word; alternatively analysable as HIGH/LOW register tones with a toneless first vowel and a floating word-final toneme). The author explicitly reports no detectable word stress: impressions of stress reduced on checking to pitch (falling or high) or vowel length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; no stress of any kind is posited.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. For tone: first vowel of a word is extremely short and quality-neutralized (sections 2.2, 10.2), and phonetically its pitch is conditioned by the preceding word's final toneme; long final syllable nuclei carry one toneme, long initial nuclei carry two.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level observation (loudness differences 'between the syllables of a word'); pitch contours described for words in sandhi-free frames and utterance-final position (final intoneme).
new_statements.identity_note: Healey 1964 describes Telefol as spoken around Telefomin (Sandaun Province), data from fieldwork 1959-1964; the OPD lists the same variety (Teléfól/Telefolmin). No dialect split relevant to the statement; glottocode tele1256.

sources.note: Dedicated section 7.3 'Stress' (p. 28): author could not detect any consistent loudness differences between syllables of a word; apparent 'stress' turned out to be falling/high pitch or long vowels. Language analysed with two tonemes UP (acute) and DOWN (grave), one per short syllable nucleus (section 7, pp. 26ff); alternative HIGH/LOW register analysis with toneless first vowel and floating final toneme (section 10.2, pp. 48-49).

sources.note: Front matter section 6 'Alphabet' (p. xvi): tone 'is thoroughly contrastive' and is marked (acute = up toneme, unmarked = down toneme; hacek/circumflex for down-up / up-down on long vowels). Nothing said about stress (read pp. i-xvii).
